content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It is a life-limiting, multisystem disease that affects over 70,000 individuals globally. Between 80% and 90% of individuals with CF experience pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI). If left untreated, PEI leads to poor nutritional status, which can have significant negative effects on overall health. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) has been shown to improve nutritional status, which is associated with better lung function in individuals with CF. However, there is no standardized protocol for the timing of PERT administration in relation to meals, leading to variability in dosing practices. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and effectiveness of different PERT dosing strategies based on the timing of administration. Efficacy was assessed in terms of fat absorption, while effectiveness was evaluated through measures such as nutritional status, lung function, and quality of life. To achieve this, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. The search was last updated on June 24, 2021. Additionally, ongoing trial registries were searched on July 9, 2021. The reference lists of relevant articles and reviews were also examined. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), including cross-over RCTs with a minimum washout period of two weeks, as well as quasi-RCTs that investigated PERT dosing regimens in individuals of any age with CF. Two independent authors screened and assessed the studies identified during the search. The authors planned to use the GRADE approach to evaluate the certainty of evidence for critical outcomes. However, no eligible studies were identified for inclusion in the review. The main results of the review revealed that no studies met the eligibility criteria. The excluded studies either used a cross-over design without an adequate washout period between treatments or did not specifically assess the timing of PERT administration. One study, which was terminated early, is awaiting further assessment pending additional information. The authors concluded that they were unable to determine whether one PERT dosing schedule is superior to another due to the lack of eligible RCTs. While PERT has been shown to improve nutritional status in individuals with CF, there is a limited body of research addressing the specific question of dosing timing. Malnutrition and gastrointestinal symptoms remain common in CF, and further research is needed to evaluate the impact of different PERT dosing schedules on fat absorption and other outcomes. Future studies should also aim to establish reliable outcome measures and define minimal clinically important differences. Although cross-over RCTs may offer advantages over parallel group designs, it is essential to include an adequate washout period between intervention phases to ensure reliable results.
